lead: The Carnot cycle is a closed loop of four reversible steps run between a hot reservoir at T₁ and a cold reservoir at T₂. It is the best engine possible between those two temperatures. Every real engine, from a Chennai backup generator to a coal power plant, is judged against it. Its efficiency depends only on T₁ and T₂, not on the gas, the size of the machine or the pressures used.
prereq: You need: reversible processes, and the isothermal and adiabatic work formulas for an ideal gas.

blocks.text: Take m kg of ideal gas in a piston-cylinder. The hot reservoir is at T₁ and the cold reservoir at T₂. Every step is reversible: no friction, no finite temperature gap, no unrestrained expansion. Define Q₁ as heat taken in and Q₂ as heat rejected, both positive magnitudes.

items: 1→2 isothermal expansion at T₁. The gas touches the hot reservoir, takes Q₁, and does work. T stays T₁.
2→3 adiabatic expansion. The gas is insulated. It expands further, does work, and T falls from T₁ to T₂. A reversible adiabatic step is isentropic (see entropy).
3→4 isothermal compression at T₂. The gas touches the cold reservoir. Work goes in and the gas rejects Q₂ at constant T₂.
4→1 adiabatic compression. The gas is insulated. Work goes in and T rises from T₂ back to T₁. The gas returns to state 1.

blocks.text: On a p-V diagram the path is two isotherms cut by two adiabats. The enclosed area is the net work per cycle.
For an ideal gas, the two isothermal heat transfers have fixed forms. The two adiabatic steps link their volumes.
Q₁ = m R T₁ ln(V₂/V₁),   Q₂ = m R T₂ ln(V₃/V₄)
blocks.where: m is mass in kg; R is the gas constant in kJ/(kg·K); T is absolute temperature in K; V₁ to V₄ are total volumes in m³; Q₂ is the positive magnitude rejected.

blocks.text: The adiabatic steps obey TV<sup>γ−1</sup> = constant, where γ = c<sub>p</sub>/c<sub>v</sub> is the ratio of specific heats: T₁V₂<sup>γ−1</sup> = T₂V₃<sup>γ−1</sup> for 2→3 and T₁V₁<sup>γ−1</sup> = T₂V₄<sup>γ−1</sup> for 4→1. Divide the first by the second: (V₂/V₁)<sup>γ−1</sup> = (V₃/V₄)<sup>γ−1</sup>, so V₂/V₁ = V₃/V₄. The logarithms in Q₁ and Q₂ are then equal and cancel in Q₂/Q₁ = T₂/T₁.

blocks.where: η is thermal efficiency; W=Q₁−Q₂ is net work per cycle; T₁ and T₂ must be in kelvin.

blocks.text: The result holds for every working substance, not only a gas. A derivation on one substance is enough because Carnot's theorem says the reversible efficiency is fixed by the reservoirs.

items: No engine working between two fixed reservoirs can be more efficient than a reversible engine working between the same two reservoirs.
All reversible engines working between the same two reservoirs have the same efficiency, whatever the working substance, the size of the cycle or the pressures used.

blocks.text: Some syllabi call the whole result Carnot’s principle and list part 2 as a corollary. Both parts are proved by contradiction. Part 1. Suppose an engine X between the two reservoirs were more efficient than a reversible engine R. Let both take the same Q₁ from the hot reservoir, so X gives more work: WX > WR. Run R backwards as a refrigerator, driven by WR taken from X’s output: it puts exactly Q₁ back into the hot reservoir. The hot reservoir is now unchanged, and the pair delivers the surplus WX − WR as work, all drawn from the cold reservoir. That is a PMM2, forbidden by the Kelvin-Planck statement. Part 2. Let X be a second reversible engine. The same argument shows X cannot beat R; X is reversible too, so running X backwards shows R cannot beat X. Their efficiencies are equal.

A real engine between T₁ and T₂ has irreversibilities and lower efficiency. The Carnot value 1−T₂/T₁ is the upper limit, not a promise. It is the benchmark used to judge power plants and refrigerators.

figure.caption: The worked example’s Carnot cycle on 1 kg of air between 900 K and 300 K. Left: the four states it passes through (the p-V shape is a sketch, because the volume grows thirtyfold). Right: the same cycle on T-S axes is a rectangle 0.199 kJ/K wide; its parts are W = 119.4 kJ and Q₂ = 59.7 kJ.

spec.aria: Left: a p-V sketch of the Carnot cycle with states 1 to 4 and their volumes and pressures, heat in along 1 to 2 at 900 K and out along 3 to 4 at 300 K. Right: a temperature-entropy rectangle from 300 K to 900 K and 0.199 kJ/K wide, the upper part labelled work 119.4 kJ and the lower part heat rejected 59.7 kJ.

examples.question: 1 kg of air (R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K), γ = 1.4) runs a Carnot cycle between 900 K and 300 K. The isothermal expansion at 900 K takes the volume from 0.1 m³ to 0.2 m³. Find Q₁, Q₂, W and η, and the volumes at the other two corners of the cycle.
steps: Data: m = 1 kg, R = 0.287 kJ/(kg·K), T₁ = 900 K, T₂ = 300 K, V₁ = 0.1 m³, V₂ = 0.2 m³. For the two adiabatic steps, V₃/V₄ = V₂/V₁ = 0.2/0.1 = 2.
Corner volumes from TV<sup>γ−1</sup> = constant: V₄ = V₁(T₁/T₂)<sup>1/(γ−1)</sup> = 0.1 × 3<sup>2.5</sup> = 0.1 × 15.59 = 1.559 m³, and V₃ = V₂ × 15.59 = 3.118 m³ (check V₃/V₄ = 2).

Pressures from p = mRT/V: p₁ = 258.3/0.1 = 2583 kPa and p₃ = 86.1/3.118 = 27.6 kPa. The gas swells about 31 times and the pressure falls about 94 times for only 119.4 kJ of work, about 39.6 kJ per m³ swept. This is why no practical engine runs a Carnot cycle on a gas.
examples.answer: Q₁ = 179.0 kJ, Q₂ = 59.7 kJ, W = 119.4 kJ and η = 66.7%; the cycle reaches V₃ = 3.118 m³ and V₄ = 1.559 m³.
examples.check:
import math
m = 1.0
R = 0.287
T1 = 900.0
T2 = 300.0
V1 = 0.1
V2 = 0.2
r = V2 / V1
Q1 = m * R * T1 * math.log(r)
Q2 = m * R * T2 * math.log(r)
W = Q1 - Q2
eta = 1 - T2 / T1
print(round(Q1, 1))
print(round(Q2, 1))
print(round(W, 1))
print(round(eta * 100, 1))

traps: Temperatures must be in kelvin. Using °C in 1−T₂/T₁ gives a meaningless number. Convert first.
Efficiency is a ratio of energies per cycle. It does not depend on m or on the cycle's size; do not multiply η by mass.
Q₂ in 1−Q₂/Q₁ is the positive heat rejected. If your first-law sign convention makes Q₂ negative, do not subtract a negative by mistake.
An efficiency above 1−T₂/T₁ is impossible for any engine between those reservoirs. Equality means reversible; a real engine is lower.
The Carnot cycle is not a real Rankine or Brayton cycle. Those cycles come later in this subject; do not use their practical efficiencies as Carnot limits.

quiz.q: State the four steps of a Carnot cycle run on a gas between T₁ and T₂. Say which steps take in or reject heat.
quiz.a: Isothermal expansion at T₁ takes in Q₁. Adiabatic expansion cools the gas from T₁ to T₂. Isothermal compression at T₂ rejects Q₂. Adiabatic compression returns the gas from T₂ to T₁. All steps are reversible.

quiz.q: Why can the efficiency of a Carnot cycle be written using only reservoir temperatures, although Q₁ and Q₂ depend on the gas and volumes?
quiz.a: For a reversible cycle between the same two reservoirs, the ratio Q₂/Q₁ is fixed at T₂/T₁. The volume ratios in Q₁ and Q₂ are equal, so gas properties and volumes cancel.

quiz.q: A Carnot engine works between 500 K and 300 K. Find its efficiency.
A Carnot engine takes Q₁ = 100 kJ from a 600 K reservoir and rejects heat at 300 K. Find the maximum η, Q₂ and W.
An inventor claims an efficiency of 70% between 800 K and 300 K. Check the claim.
quiz.a: The Carnot limit is 1 − 300/800 = 0.625 = 62.5%. The claim 70% is above 62.5%, so it is impossible for any engine between these reservoirs.

quiz.q: Two reversible engines work between the same two reservoirs. One uses air, the other helium; their sizes differ. Compare their efficiencies and Q₂/Q₁ ratios.
quiz.a: Both have η = 1−T₂/T₁ and Q₂/Q₁ = T₂/T₁. Substance and size do not matter for reversible engines between fixed reservoirs.

quiz.q: Why must the temperatures in 1−T₂/T₁ be absolute temperatures?
quiz.a: The ratio Q₂/Q₁ equals T₂/T₁ only on the absolute scale. Celsius zero is arbitrary and can give negative or meaningless ratios. Use kelvin.

beyond: Not for the exam. Power-plant designers use the Carnot limit as the target that no real cycle can beat; irreversibilities and finite temperature differences are charged as exergy loss in the topic of available energy. Refrigerator and heat-pump ratings use the same reversible limit in coefficient-of-performance form. Search next for Carnot efficiency, exergy analysis and T-s diagram of a power cycle.
